author: Irina Velitskaya
title: Mother Russia Is Mentally Ill - Commentary Magazine
text:
The other day, on my usual stroll through the absurdist universe of social media, I came across a video clip of the kind that tends to go viral faster than almost any other: the depiction of a foolish person being humiliated.
In the clip, a young Russian soldier, evidently a new recruit, is attempting to fire a YakB-12.7 helicopter machine gun during a training session. The YakB-12.7 is a gas-operated, turret-mounted rotating gun introduced in 1973 and still widely used by the Russian Army. (I am tempted to say “what remains of the Russian Army.”) Somehow, the recruit handles the gun incorrectly, and the recoil spins him wildly around the turret like a cartoon squirrel caught in the spokes of a speeding bicycle—and then he is flung, limbs flailing, into the air. In the background, as the unmanned gun continues to spin, barely missing his instructor, we can hear the shouts and scattered laughter of the other troops. The soldier was evidently uninjured because, in classic Russian fashion, the machine gun had been badly jury-rigged for use not in a helicopter but on top of a truck.
The video, verified as genuine by several pro-Russian media channels, instantly transported me to scenes from my childhood in Sinegorskiy, a ragged settlement in southwestern Russia: rowdy youths hanging off of the sides of careening ATVs and jet skis, leaping off of lakeside cliffs or being shoved by “friends” down rock-strewn hills, throwing vodka bottles at one another’s heads, and crashing into other vehicles and trees and each other. They were bored and foolhardy and hot-blooded like small-town adolescent boys anywhere in the world but with a uniquely Russian admixture of fatalism and barely suppressed suicidal urges. Crucially, these urges were not overtly depressive; rather, they were of the sort that professed genuine amusement at the prospect of imminent death. But they didn’t laugh at death because they were brave; they laughed because they didn’t care.
It is these qualities, seeping upward from below—from 10,000 other hamlets like Sinegorskiy across the vast expanse of Russia and its ethnic enclaves—that have determined the course of Russia’s catastrophic war against Ukraine every bit as much as Vladimir Putin’s catastrophic decision-making from above.
_____________
As of this writing, Russia is losing eight troops for every one Ukrainian fatality, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, and Russian troop deaths now stand at more than 450,000, with total casualties as high as 1.4 million.
It’s commonly accepted by military analysts, including those who are pro-Russia, that Russia’s disastrous and bloody fiasco in Ukraine is attributable to two primary factors: first, its “cannon meat” strategy of throwing unprepared troops into grinding engagements that gain them little or no territory, and second, its utter failure to adapt to Ukraine’s increasingly sophisticated battle tactics, in particular its drone-warfare program.
A third factor, less discussed, is that Ukraine is fighting for its sovereignty while Russia is fighting for, well, nothing.
But from a practical and strategic standpoint, the question is: Why has Russia, ostensibly a modern, First World nation, failed so humiliatingly? As someone who endured the first 25 years of her life in Russia, I can state with confidence that the answer lies in the unique psyche of Russians, and in particular a toxic combination of fatalism and superstition. This is inculcated into Russians at an early age, telling them that nothing they do matters against the forces, whether mystical or divine or bureaucratic, that are arrayed against them. Hence the helpless laughter and hopeless apathy at the prospect of imminent death.
It’s called “От судьбы не уйдешь” (“Ot sudyby ne uydesh”) in Russian, which means, in a literal sense, “you can’t run away from fate.” But while that notion is common enough in many other cultures, in Russian it has a particularly bitter tang to it, for nowhere is there any implication of “dying for a greater good,” or “for a noble sacrifice,” or merely “peaceful acceptance” of what is to come. Its actual meaning, in a Russian context, is profoundly cynical: The efforts of the individual or even large groups of individuals are useless and worthless.
There is of course a vast historical heritage of subjugation that has molded the Russian mind into a kind of malleable clay. But even if one ignores the psychological impact on ordinary Russians of centuries of czarist or Communist rule, there is a simpler and homelier explanation. It is as small and as insignificant as a pin.
Once, when she was weeding her watermelon patch, my mother found a common darning pin in the dirt. I was just a little girl at the time, but I still can recall her terrified shriek, for a stray needle or pin found on one’s property meant that a death curse had been pronounced. She raced into our cabin for some rubber gloves—it isn’t easy to pick up a needle with gardening gloves—built a small bonfire from household trash, and cast the tissue-wrapped pin into the flames, screaming imprecations against all of her many enemies.
And yet, if it were a real curse, and my mother had failed to discover the pin or to burn it, and had subsequently suffered a fatal apoplexy of otherworldly origins, she would have bowed obediently to death.
If all this sounds somewhat insane, well, my mother is, in fact, seriously askew. Yet there is no one in Sinegorskiy who would have been even slightly taken aback by my mother’s witchy ritual. Indeed, while it’s possible that the needle was one my mother had herself dropped at some point previously, it’s more likely that it actually was placed there by one of her enemy neighbors. And that is sobering, for if my mother is unbalanced and irrational, so then is most of Sinegorskiy.
Now, multiply my mother by some significant portion of Russia’s population of 140 million people. Not everyone is superstitious, of course, but in the smaller towns and in the “ethnic” republics like Chechnya from where so many military recruits are drawn, superstition is rife. My mother, upon leaving our cabin at dawn, would curse vehemently if the first person she saw was a woman, for that was a harbinger of ill fortune. If someone mistakenly wished her a happy birthday before the actual date of her birthday, it was tantamount to being threatened with a razor to her throat.
Even laughter of any sort was not allowed in our cabin because that, too, would bring ill luck down upon our heads. And none of this is superstition in the American sense of “a broken mirror means seven years of bad luck.” After all, that’s nothing more than a folk saying, and we throw the mirror away and forget about it. No, the Russian belief in superstition is deadly serious and, in smaller towns, all-pervasive. It is so prevalent, in fact, that at some point one must conclude that an utterly unquestioning investment in the forces of superstition becomes indistinguishable from insanity.
These are the people who are being recruited to fight in Ukraine, and who go willingly to their deaths. If one can die because of the power of a stray needle, then one is infinitely more helpless against the power of the state and the Ukrainian foe.
It should go without saying that everything that happens to a person can be attributed to only two general phenomena: things the person does (or doesn’t do) that are in his control and things that are outside of his control. The course of civilization is the progressive exertion of the force of the former over the latter.
In that sense, Russian civilization is slipping backward into the mire. It’s profoundly egotistical, in a very narrow understanding, to believe that one can curse another human being by means of needles and imprecations. But it’s even more profoundly self-diminishing to believe that one has no actual power in the real world to affect the course of events, or even one’s own life, by means of rational action.
So countless thousands of young men continue to shuffle numbly into the Russian war machine after as little as 10 days of training, and a large percentage of them are destined to die in Ukraine on behalf of a cause that has been long since forgotten. A significant percentage of these deaths occur, according to some estimates, within mere minutes of the recruits’ first combat engagement.
And their mothers, girlfriends, and widows will shrug helplessly when they learn of these inevitable and pointless deaths and will point with pride at the fancy memorial plaques the Russian government sends them.
This cycle shows no signs of slowing down for, as I see it from my place of permanent refuge in America, Mother Russia is mentally ill.
